content:
Planning to open a PR adding MeasureTheory.poincare_1d for f: ℝ → ℝ with ContDiff ℝ 1 f and f.support ⊆ Ioo a b, 

∫ t in Icc a b, f t ^ 2 ≤ (b - a) ^ 2 * ∫ t in Icc a b, (deriv f t) ^ 2

It's the base case for the n-dim convex-domain version (Fubini over coordinate slices), which I plan to upstream as a follow-up. A few questions I'd like input on before opening the PR:

  1. Placement. I have it at Mathlib/Analysis/FunctionalSpaces/PoincareInequality.lean, alongside SobolevInequality.lean. The namespace is MeasureTheory (matches CurveIntegral/Poincare.lean). Would Mathlib/MeasureTheory/... be preferred? Or split (helper in MeasureTheory/, main statement in Analysis/FunctionalSpaces/)?
  2. Statement form. Raw-integral form as shown, or eLpNorm f 2 μ-based? My reading is that the raw form is cleaner for an explicit-constant inequality, and the eLpNorm wrapper can live in a follow-up. Preference either way?
  3. Support hypothesis. f.support ⊆ Ioo a b, tsupport f ⊆ Ioo a b, or HasCompactSupport f + tsupport f ⊆ Icc a b? HasCompactSupport strikes me as more idiomatic; open to either.
  4. Regularity hypothesis. ContDiff ℝ 1 f (global) or ContDiffOn ℝ 1 f (Icc a b) (local)? The local version matches integral_deriv_of_contDiffOn_Icc exactly; the global version is what callers from H¹₀-approximation arguments naturally have.
  5. Helper visibility. The proof factors through
sq_integral_Ioc_le_length_mul_integral_sq_Icc :
   a ≤ x → ContinuousOn g (Icc a x) →
   (∫ t in Ioc a x, g t) ^ 2 ≤ (x - a) * ∫ t in Icc a x, g t ^ 2

(Cauchy-Schwarz v. the constant function 1, proved by the variance trick). Keep it public, mark private, or generalise to arbitrary measure spaces and keep public?

  1. I searched open PRs and upstream branches for Poincaré/Friedrichs/Sobolev-inequality work and found nothing in flight (the existing Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Integral/CurveIntegral/Poincare.lean is the Poincaré lemma for 1-forms). Flagging in case there is unpublished work: anyone have a branch with which I should coordinate?
The raw integral form is good. You should only assume ContDiffOn ℝ 1 f (Ioo a b) and ContinuousOn f (Icc a b) and f a = 0 and f b = 0 (no support assumption).

Thanks @Sébastien Gouëzel. Let f be f(x) = (x - a)^(1/3) * (b - x)^(1/3): continuous on [a,b], C^1 on (a,b), and f a = f b = 0. Near a, the first derivative behaves like (x - a)^(-2/3), so (deriv f)^2 behaves like (x - a)^(-4/3), which is not integrable on [a,b]. Should I add something like IntervalIntegrable (fun t => (deriv f t) ^2) volume a b to the hypothesis list?

No. The thing is that you should write things with ||f x||_e^2, i.e., using extended norms, and the Lebesgue integral. For estimates, that's most often the right thing to do as we learnt in Carleson. An added benefit is that you can then state it for a function taking values in an arbitrary normed space, not just ℝ
Ahh makes sense, will do. Thank you!
Follow-up: https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/40824 PR submitted here. I ended up dropping f b = 0 because it was unused.
Could you do some have-folding so it looks less like AI generated?

Some quick comments. @Alejandro Soto Franco

  1. There's nothing special about 2 here and you should prove your inequality for any 1≤p≤∞ by using holder's inequality instead of cauchy-schwarz.
  2. Related to the first point. You basically first proved that for all x within Ioo a b, ‖f x‖ₑ ≤ ∫⁻ t in Ioc a x, ‖deriv f t‖ₑ. I think this deserves to be a theorem for its own sake because from here you can prove that there exists a constant C such that for any reasonable f, ∫⁻ x in Icc a b, ‖f x‖ₑ ^ p ≤ C * ∫⁻ x in Icc a b, ‖deriv f x‖ₑ ^ q for any p, q between 1 and ∞(as if L∞L^\inftyL∞ norm is controlled by L1L^1L1 norm, then all LpL^pLp and LqL^qLq norms control each other).

  3. As you mentioned above, this theorem does not require f b = 0. However, if you indeed assume f b = 0, then you can obtain the following better result
    ∫ t in Icc a b, ‖f t‖ₑ^ p ≤ 2⁻¹ * (b - a) ^ p * ∫ t in Icc a b, ‖deriv f x‖ₑ ^ p
    by using ‖f x‖ₑ ≤ ∫⁻ t in Ioc a x, ‖deriv f t‖ₑ and its analogue ‖f x‖ₑ ≤ ∫⁻ t in Ioc x b, ‖deriv f t‖ₑ. This is another reason why I want you to extract this theorem out.

  4. It is probably better to prove the inequality first under the CompleteSpace assumption and make it a private lemma.

@Weiyi Wang sure. @Yongxi Lin (Aaron) for #1 sure, 2 was just what I was used to. #2, yeah I wanted to package this as one Poincare file but I agree I can separate that out. #3, very smart, agreed (folded into previous). #4, I went back and forth with this w a friend and was unsure about the use of a private lemma. If you feel it is more idiomatic tho I am happy to proceed with that
I think it is more idiomatic. For example, you can see how it is done in Complex.norm_deriv_le_of_forall_mem_sphere_norm_le for Cauchy's estimate.
Ah I see, much appreciated. Do you know of a good reference I can look at for Fubini on coordinate slices?
I don't know, but I think the final version that goes into mathlib should be proved for any domains such that it has bounded projection on some axis (instead of just convex domains).
Actually maybe we need both versions. :rolling_on_the_floor_laughing:
beat me to it yeah, having both seems appropriate

I am also a bit unsure about whether the approach you selected is the best one. There are also proofs of the Poincare's inequality through variational principle and calculations of the first eigenvalue of a certain ODE, and this can give optimal constant in the Poincare's inequality (of course this proof requires more machinery). Not sure whether this approach relies on the approach in your PR.

Update: after a second thought I think it is fine. Your proof is true for any normed spaces but the variational approach typically relies on Rellich compactness and is probably not true for infinite dimensional normed spaces.
